name: Lottie Moon
title: Lottie Moon: letters that made the work of mission visible
description: Lottie Moon’s teaching and evangelistic work in China, and her letters to the churches, show a mission sustained by relationships and partnership.

sections.heading: A teacher arrives in China
paragraphs: Charlotte Digges Moon was born in Virginia in 1840. She received an advanced education compared with what was possible for many women of her time, and she worked as a teacher. In 1873 she was sent to China, where her sister Edmonia had begun serving the year before.

Known as Lottie, she taught at a school for girls and visited communities to share the Christian faith with women and families. Her work took place mainly in Shandong Province. Teaching and visiting were part of a work that required a long-term presence.

sections.heading: The churches also needed to listen
paragraphs: Moon wrote letters to explain missionary life and to ask that more workers be sent and supported. The IMB archive preserves writings from that period. Her letters sought to help the churches know about needs that distance could make invisible.

She died in December 1912, after decades of service. Baptist memory linked her name to a missions offering. Before she became that symbol, she was a person who taught, wrote, and depended on a partnership that had to be renewed over the years.

reflection: Philippians 4:14–18 shows a church that takes part in Paul’s service by sharing in his needs. Mission involves both those who go and those who stand with them. Staying informed, praying, giving responsibly, and listening to the receiving communities are concrete ways of taking part.

Moon’s letters invite us to keep up an honest conversation with those who serve far away. It is good to ask about their rest, their relationships, and their struggles, not only about results. A church that supports those it sends also needs to welcome their questions and recognize their human limits.
review_note: Disputed accounts about her eating and the cause of her death are left out. Letters are not reproduced, and the later offering is not presented as a personal initiative bearing her name.
